title: Electricity demand is rising. How can the US secure energy for its dual military and civilian needs?
gist: The US commercial grid that powers military installations has no legal mechanism forcing utilities to prioritize defense facilities during shortages, even as AI, reshoring, and new weapons systems drive electricity demand higher. The authors argue Washington must change the rules, expand microreactor and grid-planning programs, and use the Pentagon as an anchor tenant for grid investment.

themes.theme: Defense grid dependence and legal gap

insights.claim: The US Department of Defense is the country's largest electricity consumer, using close to one percent of US electricity and spending more than $16 billion a year on electricity and fuel, with close to $5 billion powering domestic installations.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Scale of DOD demand makes it a potential anchor customer able to reshape utility grid investment decisions.
insights.quote: The Department of Defense (DOD) has been the country’s largest electricity consumer for decades, consuming close to one percent of electricity nationally.

insights.claim: No US federal statute, regulatory rule, or state utility code requires a utility to restore or maintain power to a military installation ahead of an ordinary residential or commercial customer.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: The absence of a defense load-priority rule is the central regulatory gap investors in grid resilience and microgrids can expect policymakers to target.
insights.quote: no federal statute, regulatory rule, or state utility code requires a utility to restore or maintain power to a military installation ahead of an ordinary residential or commercial customer.

insights.claim: A 2009 GAO review found that thirty-one of the thirty-four US installations most vulnerable to a blackout relied on commercial power grids as their primary electricity source.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Longstanding, documented dependence on fragile commercial grids frames onsite generation and microgrids as an unaddressed structural need.

insights.claim: F-35 fighter hangars require 150 percent more electricity than earlier generations of Hornet and Harrier aircraft, according to Marine Corps officials.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Modern weapons platforms are structurally raising installation power draw, tightening the civilian-military competition for capacity.
insights.quote: F-35 hangars require 150 percent more electricity than earlier generations of Hornet and Harrier aircraft.

insights.claim: US Code requires the Secretary of Defense to bring 100 percent of the energy load supporting critical missions to at least 99.9 percent availability by the end of fiscal year 2030, with the most sensitive missions held to standards as high as 99.9999 percent.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: A binding 2030 availability mandate creates a procurement pipeline for resilience, microgrid, and backup-power vendors.
insights.locator: US Code requires the Secretary of Defense

insights.claim: Congress amended the Federal Power Act in 2015 to create the Defense Critical Electric Infrastructure category, but the designation only protects information about critical lines and does not obligate a utility to restore those lines first during a shortage.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: The one purpose-built legal tool exists but is toothless, signaling where new binding legislation would land.
insights.locator: The one legal mechanism built specifically

insights.claim: The DOD and DOE still have not operationalized the defense-grid partnership promised in their September 2020 memorandum of understanding, and most federal recommendations for strengthening the program have gone unimplemented.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Bureaucratic inertia is the binding constraint, meaning near-term progress hinges on political will more than technology.
insights.locator: The one legal mechanism built specifically

insights.claim: During Winter Storm Uri in February 2021, twelve of Texas's fifteen military installations lost power for several days when grid operators imposed rolling blackouts.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Concrete precedent that grid stress directly degrades defense readiness, strengthening the case for prioritization rules.
insights.locator: The cost of delay is vulnerability

insights.claim: After Typhoon Mawar knocked out power to 98 percent of Guam customers in May 2023, Andersen Air Force Base ran resupply and evacuation missions on onsite generators and fuel reserves rather than any claim on the civilian grid.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Illustrates that onsite generation, not grid priority, is currently the only reliable defense fallback.

insights.claim: Dominion Energy's restoration order for the region serving Naval Station Norfolk lists hospitals, fire and police stations, and water treatment plants ahead of ordinary customers but does not name defense facilities at all.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Shows defense facilities are literally absent from utility priority lists, a concrete gap state regulators could close.
insights.locator: The National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners

insights.claim: California utilities have exempted national-defense government agencies from rotating outages since a 1980 CPUC decision, but the protection covers only voluntary curtailment during a supply shortage, not restoration order after storm damage.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: The lone state exception is narrow, showing even best-case protections leave a restoration gap.

insights.claim: MCAS Miramar now receives credits from San Diego Gas and Electric when it uses its own microgrid to lower regional utility demand, after a 2020 event where doing so freed enough power for about two thousand homes.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: A working model where military microgrids become grid assets with a revenue/credit stream, relevant to distributed-energy business cases.
insights.locator: Rolling blackout events in Southern California

insights.claim: Under Executive Order 14299, the Army's Janus Program must have a nuclear microreactor running on a domestic installation by September 30, 2028, and has named nine candidate sites including Fort Bragg, Fort Campbell, and Redstone Arsenal.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: A hard 2028 deadline and named sites give microreactor developers a concrete near-term defense market.
insights.locator: the Army launched the Janus Program

insights.claim: The Army intends to connect its microreactors to bases via a private wire that bypasses the commercial grid, though program specifications also require the reactors to be capable of grid-connected operation.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Private-wire behind-the-meter power signals a model that sidesteps utility priority disputes entirely.
insights.locator: the Army launched the Janus Program

insights.claim: The authors propose the DOD act as an anchor tenant for grid expansion, using early long-term capacity commitments to attract lower-cost financing for infrastructure benefiting defense facilities.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Anchor-tenant framing points to a financing structure investors and utilities could underwrite around guaranteed defense offtake.
insights.quote: The department could act as an “anchor tenant” for grid expansion that would directly benefit defense facilities, communities, and industries, attracting lower-cost financing
insights.locator: New policies should also be on the table

insights.claim: The authors recommend Congress add a defense load priority requirement to the Federal Power Act or make federal grid reliability funding conditional on states adopting a defense critical load category.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Conditioning federal funding on a defense load category is the most actionable policy lever to watch for regulatory change.
insights.locator: New policies should also be on the table
